{"self_assessment": "Impact: I proposed the fish at the start and set the direction for the table: a big, simple, right-facing outline that reads clearly from the fallen dominoes alone. I put forward the plan for splitting the work across body, fin and tail, which let us build in parallel without crowding each other. I also drew the fin and the forked tail on the pad and laid the top tail lobe myself, which gave the fish the features that make it recognizable as a fish.

Execution: I sketched the fin and tail strokes so they branch gently off the body lines, which suits how dominoes pass the fall. I traced my tail lobe from the pad, and it connected to the run. I inspected the fin area closely several times and located the single jammed domino that was stopping the fin from catching, and I reported it clearly so it could be fixed. Before the push, the start was tracing through nearly all of the standing dominoes, including the body, both tail lobes and the fin.

Collaboration: I kept communication clear and specific. I assigned strokes by name, thanked teammates when they took on pieces, and told people when a stretch was already covered so we avoided duplicate work. I asked everyone to keep hands off the body after it was connected so nothing got bumped before the push, and I kept my own hands off during that stretch.

Leadership: I took charge at the start by choosing the animal and setting the plan, then kept the table coordinated on who owned which stroke. In the final stretch I helped keep the group focused on protecting what was already working. The result was a connected fish finished with time to spare.", "my_share_percent": 30}
